title: False friends
description: Words that look like Spanish but mean something different. The #1 trap for Spanish speakers learning English.

rounds.exampleEn: Actually, I don't think that works.
rounds.exampleEs: En realidad, creo que eso no funciona.
rounds.commonMistake: actualmente, no creo que eso funcione.
rounds.explanation: "Actually" emphasizes what is true. "Actualmente" = currently / right now.

rounds.exampleEn: We eventually got there on time.
rounds.exampleEs: Finalmente llegamos a tiempo.
rounds.explanation: "Eventually" = after some time, in the end. "Eventualmente" = possibly, in some cases.

rounds.exampleEn: I'm so embarrassed right now.
rounds.exampleEs: Estoy tan avergonzado ahora mismo.
rounds.explanation: Famous false friend. "Embarrassed" = vergüenza (el sentimiento). "Embarazada" = pregnant.

rounds.exampleEn: I didn't realize it was so late.
rounds.exampleEs: No me di cuenta de que era tan tarde.
rounds.commonMistake: no me di cuenta de que era tan tarde.
rounds.explanation: "Realize" = to become aware of. "Realizar" = to carry out, perform (in the sense of "do").

rounds.exampleEn: Let me introduce my colleague, Ana.
rounds.exampleEs: Permíteme presentar a mi colega, Ana.
rounds.commonMistake: permíteme introducir a mi colega, Ana.
rounds.explanation: "Introduce (a person)" = presentar. "Introducir" (object/concept) = to bring in, to insert.

rounds.exampleEn: That's a sensible plan.
rounds.exampleEs: Ese es un plan razonable.
rounds.explanation: "Sensible" = reasonable, showing good judgment. In Spanish, "sensible" = sensitive.

rounds.exampleEn: This is a sensitive issue. Please be careful.
rounds.exampleEs: Este es un tema delicado. Por favor, ten cuidado.
rounds.explanation: "Sensitive" = emotionally aware, or requiring careful handling. The Spanish "sensible" = reasonable.

rounds.exampleEn: I'm sorry for your loss. I'm very sympathetic.
rounds.exampleEs: Lamento tu pérdida. Te acompaño en el sentimiento.
rounds.explanation: "Sympathetic" = feeling compassion. "Simpático" in Spanish = nice, friendly. In English, "nice" or "pleasant".

rounds.exampleEn: She won the singing contest.
rounds.exampleEs: Ella ganó el concurso de canto.
rounds.commonMistake: ella ganó el contestar de canto.
rounds.explanation: "Contest" (noun) = competition. "Contestar" = to answer. The verb in English is "to contest" (to challenge).

rounds.exampleEn: The book was a great success.
rounds.exampleEs: El libro fue un gran éxito.
rounds.commonMistake: el libro fue un gran suceso.
rounds.explanation: "Success" = achieving something good. "Suceso" in Spanish = event, happening.

rounds.exampleEn: Could you assist me with this, please?
rounds.exampleEs: ¿Podrías ayudarme con esto, por favor?
rounds.explanation: "Assist" = to help. "Asistir" in Spanish = to attend (an event).

rounds.exampleEn: I'll attend the meeting tomorrow.
rounds.exampleEs: Asistiré a la reunión mañana.
rounds.explanation: "Attend" = to be present at, to go to. "Atender" in Spanish = to serve, to help (a customer).

rounds.exampleEn: I've been constipated for three days.
rounds.exampleEs: Llevo tres días estreñido.
rounds.explanation: Classic! "Constipated" in English = difficulty going to the bathroom. "Constipado" in Spanish = having a cold.

rounds.exampleEn: I have a cold. I can't stop sneezing.
rounds.exampleEs: Tengo un resfriado. No puedo parar de estornudar.
rounds.explanation: "I have a cold" = tengo un resfriado. "I have a calor" doesn't exist — use "I'm hot" instead.

rounds.exampleEn: Push the door, don't pull.
rounds.exampleEs: Empuja la puerta, no tires.
rounds.explanation: Wait — this is CORRECT! "Push" = empujar. But "pull" = tirar. The mistake is using "tirar" (pull) for "push". Common confusion because "tirar" in Spanish is much broader.

rounds.exampleEn: She looks younger, but she's actually 50.
rounds.exampleEs: Parece más joven, pero en realidad tiene 50.
rounds.commonMistake: parece más joven, pero actualmente tiene 50.
rounds.explanation: Same as ff-1, with a clearer example. "Currently 50" would mean she was 50 before, isn't now.

rounds.exampleEn: It's a long way to the station.
rounds.exampleEs: Es un largo camino a la estación.
rounds.commonMistake: (no common mistake — this is a true cognate)
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE! "Largo" = long in both languages. Some words actually do match. This is a control example — not all lookalikes are false friends.

rounds.exampleEn: The food was exquisite.
rounds.exampleEs: La comida estuvo exquisita.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Both mean the same. Sometimes the false-friend trap itself is the false friend — this word is fine.

rounds.exampleEn: I sent my job application yesterday.
rounds.exampleEs: Envié mi solicitud de trabajo ayer.
rounds.commonMistake: envié mi aplicación de trabajo ayer.
rounds.explanation: "Application" = both "app" (software) AND "formal request" (job application). In Spanish, "aplicación" usually means only the software. For job/school requests, use "solicitud".

rounds.exampleEn: Can you record the meeting?
rounds.exampleEs: ¿Puedes grabar la reunión?
rounds.explanation: "To record" = to capture on tape. "Recordar" in Spanish = to remember. For memory, use "to remember" in English.

rounds.exampleEn: I don't remember his name.
rounds.exampleEs: No recuerdo su nombre.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Both mean to recall. Watch out: don't confuse with "to record" (grabar).

rounds.exampleEn: The actual cost was much higher than the estimate.
rounds.exampleEs: El costo real fue mucho más alto que el presupuesto.
rounds.commonMistake: el costo actual fue mucho más alto.
rounds.explanation: Classic! "Actual" in English = real, true (not made up). "Actual" in Spanish = current, present. For "current" in English, use "current" or "present".

rounds.exampleEn: She's currently working on a new project.
rounds.exampleEs: Actualmente está trabajando en un proyecto nuevo.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Both mean at this moment. The trap is the OTHER way: "actually" doesn't mean "actualmente".

rounds.exampleEn: Please notify me when the package arrives.
rounds.exampleEs: Por favor notifícame cuando llegue el paquete.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning, same use. Not all lookalikes are false friends.

rounds.exampleEn: Stop ignoring me!
rounds.exampleEs: ¡Deja de ignorarme!
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Both mean to pay no attention.

rounds.exampleEn: I need a large coffee, please.
rounds.exampleEs: Quiero un café grande, por favor.
rounds.explanation: "Large" = big in size. "Largo" in Spanish = long (in length, duration). For long, use "long" in English.

rounds.exampleEn: It's a long walk to the station.
rounds.exampleEs: Es un largo camino a la estación.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Both mean long in length or time. The trap is "large" (size) in English doesn't mean "largo".

rounds.exampleEn: My parents live in Madrid.
rounds.exampleEs: Mis padres viven en Madrid.
rounds.explanation: "Parents" = father and mother. "Parientes" in Spanish = relatives (any family members). For relatives, use "relatives" in English.

rounds.exampleEn: I have relatives all over Spain.
rounds.exampleEs: Tengo parientes por toda España.
rounds.explanation: "Relatives" = family members. "Relativos" in Spanish = things relating to something (relative pronouns).

rounds.exampleEn: Stop pretending you don't know!
rounds.exampleEs: ¡Deja de fingir que no lo sabes!
rounds.commonMistake: deja de pretender que no lo sabes.
rounds.explanation: "Pretend" = to make believe. "Pretender" in Spanish = to try, to intend ("pretendo ir" = I intend to go).

rounds.exampleEn: She attempted to climb the mountain.
rounds.exampleEs: Intentó escalar la montaña.
rounds.explanation: "Attempt" = to try. "Atentar" in Spanish = to commit an act against ("atentar contra la vida").

rounds.exampleEn: We reached a compromise. He works mornings, I work afternoons.
rounds.exampleEs: Llegamos a un acuerdo. Él trabaja mañanas, yo trabajo tardes.
rounds.explanation: "Compromise" in English = middle ground. "Compromiso" in Spanish = commitment, engagement, promise. For that, use "commitment" in English.

rounds.exampleEn: Marriage is a big commitment.
rounds.exampleEs: El matrimonio es un gran compromiso.
rounds.commonMistake: el matrimonio es un gran compromiso (in the English sense).
rounds.explanation: "Commitment" = a promise or dedication. The English "compromise" is NOT this — it's a middle ground.

rounds.exampleEn: I just realized I left my keys at home.
rounds.exampleEs: Acabo de darme cuenta de que dejé las llaves en casa.
rounds.commonMistake: acabo de realizar que dejé las llaves.
rounds.explanation: Same as ff-4. "Realizar" in Spanish = to carry out, to do ("realizar un proyecto").

rounds.exampleEn: I expect we'll be there by 8.
rounds.exampleEs: Espero que estemos ahí a las 8.
rounds.explanation: "Expect" = to anticipate, to look forward to. "Esperar" in Spanish can mean both "to wait" and "to hope/expect".

rounds.exampleEn: If you work hard, you will succeed.
rounds.exampleEs: Si trabajas duro, tendrás éxito.
rounds.explanation: "Succeed" = to achieve a goal. "Suceder" in Spanish = to happen. For that, use "to happen" in English.

rounds.exampleEn: The emergency exit is on your left.
rounds.exampleEs: La salida de emergencia está a tu izquierda.
rounds.explanation: "Exit" = a way out. "Éxito" in Spanish = success. They look similar but mean different things.

rounds.exampleEn: I want to leave the country.
rounds.exampleEs: Quiero salir del país.
rounds.explanation: "Salir" = to go out, to leave. The English "to leave" is the same meaning. The mistake is using "dejar" (to leave something behind) for "salir" (to go out).

rounds.exampleEn: Please remove your shoes at the door.
rounds.exampleEs: Por favor quítate los zapatos en la puerta.
rounds.explanation: "Remove" = to take away. "Remover" in Spanish = to stir, to mix. In Latin America, some countries use "remover" for both — be aware of the difference.

rounds.exampleEn: Please inform me when it's ready.
rounds.exampleEs: Por favor infórmame cuando esté listo.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. Not all lookalikes are false friends.

rounds.exampleEn: They constructed a new building downtown.
rounds.exampleEs: Construyeron un edificio nuevo en el centro.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. Etymologically the same word.

rounds.exampleEn: I study at the library every afternoon.
rounds.exampleEs: Estudio en la biblioteca cada tarde.
rounds.explanation: "Library" = a place with books to borrow. "Librería" in Spanish = a bookstore (where you buy books).

rounds.exampleEn: I bought this novel at the bookstore.
rounds.exampleEs: Compré esta novela en la librería.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. The confusion is the other direction: "library" ≠ "librería".

rounds.exampleEn: There's a stain on the carpet.
rounds.exampleEs: Hay una mancha en la alfombra.
rounds.commonMistake: hay una mancha en la carpeta.
rounds.explanation: "Carpet" = a rug on the floor. "Carpeta" in Spanish = a folder. For folder, use "folder" in English.

rounds.exampleEn: I keep my documents in this folder.
rounds.exampleEs: Guardo mis documentos en esta carpeta.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. The confusion is the other direction: "carpet" ≠ "carpeta".

rounds.exampleEn: Tie the boat to the dock with this rope.
rounds.exampleEs: Ata el barco al muelle con esta soga.
rounds.commonMistake: ata el barco con esta ropa.
rounds.explanation: "Rope" = a thick string. "Ropa" in Spanish = clothes. Easy mistake because of similar spelling.

rounds.exampleEn: The store sells winter clothing.
rounds.exampleEs: La tienda vende ropa de invierno.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. Confusion is the other direction: "rope" ≠ "ropa".

rounds.exampleEn: I love salsa dancing.
rounds.exampleEs: Me encanta bailar salsa.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning in both. Watch out for the pronunciation though — in English, it's "SAWL-sa," not "SAL-sa."

rounds.exampleEn: Will you attend the conference next week?
rounds.exampleEs: ¿Asistirás a la conferencia la próxima semana?
rounds.explanation: "Attend" = to go to, to be present at. "Atender" in Spanish = to serve, to help a customer. In Mexican Spanish, "atender" can mean to attend in the sense of "to wait on someone" (a patient, a customer).

rounds.exampleEn: I really appreciate your help.
rounds.exampleEs: Agradezco mucho tu ayuda.
rounds.explanation: "Appreciate" in English is mostly about being grateful. "Apreciar" in Spanish can mean both "to value" AND "to like." Use "to value" or "to like" in English for the second sense.

rounds.exampleEn: The company is worth 5 billion dollars.
rounds.exampleEs: La empresa vale 5 mil millones de dólares.
rounds.commonMistake: vale 5 billones de dólares (would be 5 trillion!).
rounds.explanation: In English, "billion" = 1,000,000,000 (10^9). In Spain, "billón" = 1,000,000,000,000 (10^12). Different scales! In Latin America, "billón" = 10^9 (same as English).

rounds.exampleEn: The US debt is over 30 trillion dollars.
rounds.exampleEs: La deuda de EE.UU. supera los 30 billones de dólares.
rounds.explanation: Same trap as "billion." English "trillion" = 10^12. Spanish "trillón" = 10^18. Use "billion" (10^9) and "trillion" (10^12) consistently with English.

rounds.exampleEn: The team consists of five people.
rounds.exampleEs: El equipo consiste en cinco personas.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. Preposition: "of" in English, "en" in Spanish.

rounds.exampleEn: The accident resulted in three injuries.
rounds.exampleEs: El accidente resultó en tres heridos.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. The Spanish "resultar" can also mean "to turn out" (without the consequence sense).

rounds.exampleEn: He abused his power to help his friends.
rounds.exampleEs: Abusó de su poder para ayudar a sus amigos.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. Preposition: "of" in English, "de" in Spanish.

rounds.exampleEn: It depends on the weather.
rounds.exampleEs: Depende del clima.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. Preposition: "on" in English, "de" in Spanish.

rounds.exampleEn: He made a fatal mistake.
rounds.exampleEs: Cometió un error fatal.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Both mean deadly or disastrous. In some uses, English "fatal" is more literary than Spanish "fatal".

rounds.exampleEn: She was furious when she found out.
rounds.exampleEs: Estaba furiosa cuando se enteró.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. Spanish speakers sometimes mistakenly use "furioso" for the English "furious" — but it's correct!

rounds.exampleEn: He plays golf every Sunday.
rounds.exampleEs: Juega al golf cada domingo.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same word, same pronunciation, same game.

rounds.exampleEn: I have cereal for breakfast every day.
rounds.exampleEs: Tomo cereal para desayunar cada día.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same word. Spanish speakers sometimes get the pronunciation wrong — in English, it's "SEER-ee-uhl," not "se-RE-al."

rounds.exampleEn: She edited the document before sending it.
rounds.exampleEs: Editó el documento antes de enviarlo.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. In English, "to edit" can also mean to be the editor of a newspaper.

rounds.exampleEn: The factory produces 1000 cars a day.
rounds.exampleEs: La fábrica produce 1000 coches al día.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. Also used in entertainment: "to produce a film."

rounds.exampleEn: The food was terrible.
rounds.exampleEs: La comida estaba terrible.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. In informal English, "terrible" can also mean "very bad" (not catastrophic).

rounds.exampleEn: The weather has been horrible all week.
rounds.exampleEs: El clima ha estado horrible toda la semana.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. Same as English — informal uses are common.

rounds.exampleEn: "Break a leg" is a strange idiom.
rounds.exampleEs: "Break a leg" es un modismo extraño.
rounds.commonMistake: "break a leg" es un idioma extraño.
rounds.explanation: "Idiom" in English = a fixed expression ("break a leg"). "Idioma" in Spanish = a language ("el idioma español"). For language, use "language" in English.

rounds.exampleEn: She speaks four languages fluently.
rounds.exampleEs: Habla cuatro idiomas con fluidez.
rounds.explanation: "Language" = a system of communication (Spanish, English). "Lenguaje" in Spanish = a more abstract "language" (body language, programming language). For specific languages, use "idioma" in Spanish.

rounds.exampleEn: They had a big argument about money.
rounds.exampleEs: Tuvieron una gran discusión sobre dinero.
rounds.commonMistake: tuvieron un gran argumento sobre dinero.
rounds.explanation: "Argument" in English = a disagreement. "Argumento" in Spanish = a reason or a plot summary. For the reason sense, use "argument" or "point" in English.

rounds.exampleEn: Let's have a discussion about it.
rounds.exampleEs: Hagamos una discusión sobre eso.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. Less negative than "argument" in English.

rounds.exampleEn: Oh, I just realized — it's Tuesday!
rounds.exampleEs: ¡Oh, acabo de darme cuenta — es martes!
rounds.explanation: Same as ff-4 and ff-34. Worth repeating — this is one of the most common mistakes.

rounds.exampleEn: Did you notice the new paint?
rounds.exampleEs: ¿Notaste la pintura nueva?
rounds.explanation: "Notice" = to observe. "Noticiar" in Spanish = to inform, to report news. For that, use "to inform" in English.

rounds.exampleEn: His constant humming irritates me.
rounds.exampleEs: Su tarareo constante me irrita.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. Spanish "irritar" is used the same way.

rounds.exampleEn: He was arrested for molesting children.
rounds.exampleEs: Fue arrestado por agredir a niños.
rounds.commonMistake: fue arrestado por molestar a niños.
rounds.explanation: "To molest" in English = sexual assault (a crime). "Molestar" in Spanish = to bother, to annoy. For that, use "to bother" or "to annoy" in English. The English meaning is much more serious.

rounds.exampleEn: His comments really annoy me.
rounds.exampleEs: Sus comentarios realmente me molestan.
rounds.explanation: "To annoy" = to bother, to irritate. "Enojar" in Spanish = to make angry. For that, use "to anger" or "to make angry" in English.

rounds.exampleEn: Don't embarrass me in front of my parents!
rounds.exampleEs: ¡No me avergüences frente a mis padres!
rounds.commonMistake: ¡no me embaraces frente a mis padres!
rounds.explanation: Same as ff-3. "To embarrass" = to cause shame. The Spanish "embarazar" = to impregnate. These are two of the most common false-friend mistakes.

rounds.exampleEn: Let me introduce you to my wife.
rounds.exampleEs: Permíteme presentarte a mi esposa.
rounds.explanation: Same as ff-5. For people, use "introduce." For objects, "introduce" can also work but "insert" or "bring in" is clearer.

rounds.exampleEn: I tried five times and eventually got it.
rounds.exampleEs: Lo intenté cinco veces y finalmente lo logré.
rounds.commonMistake: lo intenté cinco veces y eventualmente lo logré.
rounds.explanation: Same as ff-2. "Eventually" in English has a temporal meaning (after time). "Eventualmente" in Spanish has a probability meaning (possibly).

rounds.exampleEn: I just discovered a new restaurant.
rounds.exampleEs: Acabo de descubrir un restaurante nuevo.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. Note: "descubrir" is only for finding something that was hidden, not for finding something new (use "encontrar" for that).

rounds.exampleEn: I can't find my keys.
rounds.exampleEs: No encuentro mis llaves.
rounds.explanation: "Find" = to locate. "Fingir" in Spanish = to pretend. Easy to confuse because they start with F.

rounds.exampleEn: He faked his signature on the form.
rounds.exampleEs: Falsificó su firma en el formulario.
rounds.explanation: "To fake" = to falsify, to make something up. Not a confusion with Spanish — just a word to know.

rounds.exampleEn: I'll attend to the customer.
rounds.exampleEs: Atenderé al cliente.
rounds.commonMistake: (no mistake — true cognate in this sense)
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE in this sense. "Attend to" = to give attention to someone, to serve them. The Spanish "atender" = to serve a customer. The general "attend" without "to" = to go to (an event).

rounds.exampleEn: I have sympathy for you in this difficult time.
rounds.exampleEs: Te acompaño en el sentimiento en este momento difícil.
rounds.explanation: Same as ff-8 (the adjective). "Sympathy" = feeling of compassion. "Simpatía" in Spanish = friendliness, being likable.

rounds.exampleEn: I sympathize with your loss.
rounds.exampleEs: Te acompaño en el sentimiento por tu pérdida.
rounds.explanation: Same as ff-8 and ff-81. "To sympathize" = to feel compassion. The Spanish "simpatizar" = to like, to get along with.

rounds.exampleEn: It would be politic to wait until tomorrow.
rounds.exampleEs: Sería prudente esperar hasta mañana.
rounds.explanation: "Politic" in English (adjective, archaic but still used) = wise, prudent. "Político" in Spanish = relating to politics. For political matters, use "political" in English.

rounds.exampleEn: I need to balance work and family.
rounds.exampleEs: Necesito equilibrar trabajo y familia.
rounds.explanation: "Balance" in English = to keep things in equilibrium. "Balancear" in Spanish = to sway, to rock (a boat, a person). Same word, different connotation. For "keep in balance," use "to balance" in English.

rounds.exampleEn: Can you substitute the butter for oil?
rounds.exampleEs: ¿Puedes sustituir la mantequilla por aceite?
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. Preposition: "for" in English, "por" in Spanish.

rounds.exampleEn: The rain impeded our progress.
rounds.exampleEs: La lluvia impidió nuestro progreso.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. Preposition: "-ed" in English (transitive), takes direct object.

rounds.exampleEn: How do you pronounce this word?
rounds.exampleEs: ¿Cómo se pronuncia esta palabra?
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. Same pronunciation rules: "how do you pronounce," not "how you pronounce."

rounds.exampleEn: He pronounced the verdict in court.
rounds.exampleEs: Pronunció el veredicto en el tribunal.
rounds.explanation: Same word, two meanings in both languages: (1) to say a word, (2) to declare formally (a verdict, a sentence).

rounds.exampleEn: He defrauded the company of millions.
rounds.exampleEs: Defraudó a la empresa por millones.
rounds.commonMistake: (no mistake — true cognate in this sense)
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE in the legal sense. Note: in Spanish, "defraudar" can also mean "to disappoint" ("me defraudaste"), which has no direct English equivalent — use "to disappoint" or "to let down" instead.

rounds.exampleEn: She goes to the office every day.
rounds.exampleEs: Va a la oficina todos los días.
rounds.commonMistake: va al oficio todos los días.
rounds.explanation: "Office" in English = workplace, or a position ("the office of President"). "Oficio" in Spanish = a trade or craft ("el oficio de carpintero").

rounds.exampleEn: The officer gave me a ticket.
rounds.exampleEs: El oficial me dio una multa.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Both refer to a person in a position of authority. The Spanish "oficial" can also mean "official" (adjective).

rounds.exampleEn: He's a sane person. He makes good decisions.
rounds.exampleEs: Es una persona cuerda. Toma buenas decisiones.
rounds.explanation: "Sane" = mentally sound, reasonable. "Sano" in Spanish = physically healthy. For physical health, use "healthy" in English.

rounds.exampleEn: She eats healthy food.
rounds.exampleEs: Come comida sana.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. The confusion is the other direction: "sane" ≠ "sano."

rounds.exampleEn: What was the actual reason?
rounds.exampleEs: ¿Cuál fue la verdadera razón?
rounds.explanation: Same as ff-22. This is one of THE classic false friends. Worth repeating.

rounds.exampleEn: Can you estimate the cost?
rounds.exampleEs: ¿Puedes calcular el costo?
rounds.explanation: "Estimate" in English = to make a rough calculation. "Estimar" in Spanish can mean to calculate OR to value/esteem ("te estimo mucho" = I esteem you a lot). For the valuing sense, use "to value" or "to esteem" in English.

rounds.exampleEn: The kids pretended to be asleep.
rounds.exampleEs: Los niños fingieron estar dormidos.
rounds.explanation: Same as ff-30. Common in Spain where "pretender" often means to try/attempt.

rounds.exampleEn: The job involves a lot of travel.
rounds.exampleEs: El trabajo involucra mucho viaje.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same meaning. Preposition: "in" in English (when used passively, "involved in").

rounds.exampleEn: He climbed up the rope.
rounds.exampleEs: Subió por la cuerda.
rounds.explanation: Same as ff-46. This is one of THE classic Spanish-speaker mistakes. Worth repeating.

rounds.exampleEn: No, I don't want any.
rounds.exampleEs: No, no quiero ninguno.
rounds.explanation: TRUE COGNATE. Same word, same meaning. Both languages have a complicated double-negative system. In Spanish, "no quiero nada" = I don't want anything. In English, "I want nothing" is fine; "I don't want anything" is more natural.

rounds.exampleEn: I'd like to introduce my colleague.
rounds.exampleEs: Quisiera presentar a mi colega.
rounds.explanation: Same as ff-5 and ff-75. This is a TOP 5 mistake for Spanish speakers. Always: people = introduce, things = introduce/insert/bring in. The default Spanish-speaker reflex is to use "introducir" for both, which sounds wrong in English for people.
